chapter.name: Introduction to Trigonometry
chapter.blurb: Three right-triangle situations -- the height of the Qutub Minar, the width of a river seen from a balcony, and the altitude of a hot air balloon -- motivate trigonometry as the study of the relationship between the sides and angles of a right triangle. The chapter defines the six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle (sine, cosine, tangent and their reciprocals cosecant, secant, cotangent), shows that these ratios depend only on the angle and not on the size of the triangle, and uses the Pythagoras theorem to find every ratio once one is known. It then derives the values of all six ratios for the standard angles 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees using an isosceles right triangle and an equilateral triangle's altitude, and closes by deriving the three fundamental trigonometric identities from the Pythagoras theorem and using them to prove further identities.

concepts.name: The six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle
concepts.description: Defining sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A and cot A as ratios of the sides of a right triangle relative to an acute angle A; the reciprocal pairs and the quotient relations tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A; the notation warning that sin A is a single symbol, not a product; and the fact (from similar triangles) that these ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the right triangle.
concepts.idea: In a right triangle, the ratios of any two sides relative to one acute angle are the six trigonometric ratios of that angle, and they stay the same for every right triangle with that same angle.
concepts.rule: For right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, with acute angle A: sin A = (side opposite A) / hypotenuse = BC/AC; cos A = (side adjacent to A) / hypotenuse = AB/AC; tan A = (side opposite A) / (side adjacent to A) = BC/AB. The reciprocals are cosec A = 1/sin A = AC/BC, sec A = 1/cos A = AC/AB, cot A = 1/tan A = AB/BC. Also tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A. By the AA similarity criterion, any two right triangles with the same acute angle A give the same values for all six ratios.
concepts.example: In right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, BC is opposite angle A and AC is the hypotenuse, so sin A = BC/AC; AB is adjacent to angle A, so cos A = AB/AC (pp. 114-115).

concepts.name: Finding all trigonometric ratios from one given ratio; range constraints
concepts.description: Using the Pythagoras theorem to find the third side of a right triangle when one trigonometric ratio of an acute angle is known, then reading off all six ratios; knowing that sin A and cos A never exceed 1 while cosec A and sec A are always at least 1; and showing that equal sines (or equal cosines) of two acute angles make the angles equal.
concepts.idea: One trigonometric ratio fixes the proportion of two sides of a right triangle, and the Pythagoras theorem then supplies the third side, so every other ratio of that angle can be found.
concepts.rule: If a trigonometric ratio of angle A is given as a fraction p/q, take the two sides it relates as pk and qk for some positive number k, use the Pythagoras theorem to find the remaining side, and then write down all six ratios from the three side lengths. Because the hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle, sin A <= 1 and cos A <= 1 always, so cosec A >= 1 and sec A >= 1 always. If sin A = sin B (or cos A = cos B) for acute angles A and B, then A = B.
concepts.example: If sin A = 1/3, take the side opposite A as k and the hypotenuse as 3k; then the adjacent side is square root of (3k)^2 - k^2 = square root of 8 k^2 = 2 x square root of 2 x k, so cos A = (2 x square root of 2 x k) / 3k = (2 x square root of 2) / 3 (pp. 117-118).

concepts.idea: The values of the six ratios at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees can each be worked out from a simple triangle construction, and are worth memorising as Table 8.1.
concepts.rule: sin A takes the values 0, 1/2, 1/(square root of 2), (square root of 3)/2, 1 at A = 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees; cos A takes the same five values in reverse order. tan A = sin A / cos A gives 0, 1/(square root of 3), 1, square root of 3, and is not defined at 90 degrees (since cos 90 degrees = 0). cot A = cos A / sin A is not defined at 0 degrees (since sin 0 degrees = 0). cosec A = 1/sin A is not defined at 0 degrees; sec A = 1/cos A is not defined at 90 degrees.

Dividing by BC^2 gives cot^2 A + 1 = cosec^2 A, true for 0 degrees < A <= 90 degrees (cot A, cosec A are not defined at 0 degrees). These let one ratio be expressed in terms of another, e.g. cos A = square root of (1 - sin^2 A), or sec A = square root of (1 + tan^2 A).
